extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of poetry, drama, and classical poetics; creative writers studying Aristotelian dramatic principles
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic (and epic) poetry, with specific criteria for plot construction (complication/unravelling), use of reversal and recognition, chorus function, diction, thought, and stylistic devices. Drawn from Aristotle's Poetics as a prescriptive textbook for poets and critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complication and Unravelling (plot structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: By the Complication I mean all that extends from the beginning of the action and the part which marks the turning-point to good or bad fortune. The Unravelling is that which extends from the beginning of the change to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incidents extraneous to the action are frequently combined with a portion of the action proper to form the Complication; the rest is the Unravelling. Example: in Lynceus of Theodectes the Complication consists of incidents presupposed, seizure of the child; the Unravelling extends from accusation of murder to the end. The plot should be stated in its essential parts (e.g., the Odyssey reduced to its plot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of plot (avoid multiplicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy should not be made into an Epic structure (one with a multiplicity of plots); in drama the result of multiplicity is far from answering to the poet’s expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select portions of a larger tale rather than dramatising whole epics (e.g., dramatizing the whole Fall of Troy or whole tale of Niobe tends to fail). Keep a single, unified plot appropriate to dramatic magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal and Recognition (peripeteia & anagnorisis) as defining mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four kinds of Tragedy, depending entirely on Reversal and Recognition; identity of a tragedy is where the Complication and Unravelling are the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reversals of intention and recognitions as structural devices to produce the turning-point and consequent unravelling; both arts (tying the knot and unravelling it) must be mastered for a successful tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of tragedy (pathetic, ethical, simple, spectacle-excluded)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedies may be Pathetic (where the motive is passion), Ethical (where the motives are ethical), and Simple; the purely spectacular element is excluded from these poetic kinds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine as many poetic merits as possible (pathetic, ethical, simple) and, if not all, the greatest and most important, because critics expect excellence across lines. Examples given: tragedies on Ajax and Ixion (pathetic); Phthiotides and Peleus (ethical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and moral satisfaction in reversals
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversals of intention should produce a tragic effect that satisfies the moral sense; such an event is probable in Agathon’s sense: 'it is probable that many things should happen contrary to probability.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for outcomes (e.g., the clever rogue outwitted, brave villain defeated) that feel morally satisfying and yet plausible within the dramatic world; improbable events may be acceptable if they achieve the appropriate tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as an integral actor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be regarded as one of the actors; it should be an integral part of the whole, and share in the action, in the manner of Sophocles rather than Euripides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid choral songs that are mere interludes unrelated to the piece; choral parts should pertain to the subject and participate in the action rather than serve as detached entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (ideas and emotional effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought includes every effect produced by speech: proof and refutation; the excitation of feelings (pity, fear, anger, and the like); the suggestion of importance or its opposite, and the sense of probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat dramatic incidents and speeches from the same points of view when aiming to evoke pity, fear, importance, or probability. Incidents should be constructed so as to produce these effects without extraneous verbal exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidents should 'speak for themselves' (show, don't tell)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic incidents should be treated so that they speak for themselves without verbal exposition; the effects aimed at in speech should be produced by the speaker as a result of the speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid revealing the Thought apart from what speakers actually say; construct incidents so their significance is evident through action rather than expository speeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction vs Delivery (modes of expression belong to delivery)
rubrics_metrics.description: One branch of the inquiry treats of the Modes of Expression (what is a command, a prayer, a narrative, a threat, a question, an answer). This province belongs to the art of Delivery, and to the masters of that science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets are not seriously censured for matters properly in the domain of delivery; knowledge of modes of expression is important but distinct from poetic composition itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of style: clear without being mean
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean. The clearest style uses only current or proper words but is mean; a style wholly composed of unusual words is either a riddle or a jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieve a balance: use current/proper words for perspicuity and an infusion of rare/metaphorical/ornamental/altered forms to raise the diction above commonness. Avoid making diction wholly ordinary (mean) or wholly rare (riddle/jargon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate mixture of word-types
rubrics_metrics.description: Every word is either current, or strange, or metaphorical, or ornamental, or newly-coined, or lengthened, or contracted, or altered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a measured mixture: strange or rare words, metaphors, and ornamental terms will raise style, while proper words ensure clarity. Excessive use of rare terms becomes jargon; excessive metaphor becomes riddle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of metaphor (types and analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor is the application of an alien name by transference from genus to species, species to genus, species to species, or by analogy (proportion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphor via genus↔species and analogy/proportion; metaphors can qualify by adding the relative term; they can name relations for which there is no existing word. Employed appropriately, metaphor elevates diction; used improperly or excessively, it produces obscurity or ludicrous effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenses of speech (lengthening, contraction, alteration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthening, contraction, and alteration of words deviate in exceptional cases from the normal idiom and give distinction while partial conformity with usage gives perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics err in censuring these licenses wholesale; used with moderation they contribute to a clear yet elevated diction (examples from Epic poetry and comparisons between Aeschylus and Euripides).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in stylistic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: To employ license (metaphor, strange words, lengthening) obtrusively is grotesque; moderation is necessary in any mode of poetic diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using metaphors, rare words, or manipulations of form with the express purpose of being ludicrous or merely conspicuous; aim for proper, proportionate use to enhance beauty without producing a riddle or jargon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction's contribution to emotional and probable effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction (choice and arrangement of words) must serve Thought by helping to produce pity, fear, and a sense of probability; incidents and speeches should be crafted so diction aids these aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace or choose words (common vs rarer) to alter the perceived beauty or triviality of lines; small lexical choices can markedly affect the verse’s impact (e.g., Aeschylus vs Euripides examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence/phrase unity and construction
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence or phrase is a composite significant sound, some at least of whose parts are in themselves significant; a sentence may form unity by signifying one thing or by linking several parts together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct sentences/phrases so their unity serves the dramatic or rhetorical purpose—either to signify a single concept or to link parts into coherent narrative or argument. (Technical distinctions of letters, syllables, nouns, verbs, inflexions are noted as underlying linguistic elements.)
